title: Katakana
description: Loanwords, foreign names and menus. Often more immediately useful to a traveller than hiragana, because so much of it is English you can already understand once you can read it.

groups.title: Yōon
groups.description: Contracted sounds — consonant + small ya/yu/yo, one beat.

characters.note: Katakana is for loanwords, foreign names, onomatopoeia and emphasis — menus and product packaging are full of it.
シ (shi) vs ツ (tsu) is the classic katakana trap. シ strokes come in low and flat; ツ strokes come down from the top.
ソ (so) vs ン (n). Learn this pair together with シ/ツ.
ツ (tsu) vs シ (shi) — compare them side by side and learn them as a pair, not separately.
As the topic particle it is pronounced "wa", not "ha" — 私は = watashi wa.
Between "fu" and "hu" — the lips barely touch. ふ is the one Westerners over-pronounce.
As the direction particle it is pronounced "e", not "he".
Pronounced "o". Only ever used as the object particle, never inside a word.
Easily confused with ソ (so). ン ends low-left to high-right; ソ strokes downward.
じ and ぢ are both "ji"; じ is the one you will almost always want.
ず and づ are both "zu"; ず is the common one.
じ and ぢ are both "ji"; じ is the one you will almost always want.
ず and づ are both "zu"; ず is the common one.
Written small, read as a single beat: きゃ is one mora, not two.
